## Factorising

![](images/Q42.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

There are three kinds of factorising to consider in turn: *common factor*, *difference of two squares* and *trinomials/double brackets*. Sometimes more than one kind is needed in a single factorising question.

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$2(x+3)(x-3)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A42.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q43.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

$9m^2$ can be written as $(\dots)^2$?

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$(3m+5)(3m-5)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A43.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q44.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

*"Think of two numbers that multiple to give... and add to give..."*

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$(x-4)(x-2)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A44.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q45.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

It can help to write out all of the possible pairs of whole numbers that *multiply to give -20*.

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$(y+5)(y-4)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A45.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q46.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

Always look to take a *common factor* first. However, there may still be *more to do* afterwards...

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$3(x+3)(x-1)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A46.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q47.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

One approach is to find a pair of numbers that multiply to give 5, but that add to give -11 *when one of them is multiplied by 2 first.*

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$(2x-1)(x-5)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A47.png)

`r unhide()`

## Quadratics

![](images/Q48.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

Trying to find numbers for a solution of the form $(6x...)(x...)$ is a good place to start, but it won't work.

When that fails, try looking for a solution of the form $(3x...)(2x...)$. This means we need numbers which **multiply** to give $-5$, which also add to give $-13$ when *one of them is tripled* and *one of them is doubled*.

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$(3x+2)(x-5)$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A48.png)

`r unhide()`

## Indices

![](images/Q64.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

Learn your *index laws* carefully.

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$6x^2$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A64.png)

`r unhide()`


![](images/Q65.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$\dfrac{4}{x^2}$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A65.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q66.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

The *order of operations* means apply the *power* (of a power) before the *multiplication* (of powers).

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$\dfrac{1}{p^5}$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A66.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q67.png)

`r hide("Get a hint")`

Remember that both the $y$ *term* and the *fraction in front* are being *squared*.

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Check the answer")`

$\dfrac{9}{16}y^{10}$

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Solution - check your notes first, if stuck!")`

![](images/A67.png)

`r unhide()`

![](images/Q68.png)
